tables.caption: Disease-specific evidence for peroxisomal involvement in CNS disorders.
rows: Disease or disorder
Direct evidence and source
What the evidence supports
What remains unresolved
Implication for material evaluation
Evidence category
Alzheimer's disease
Human postmortem lipid and organelle-distribution abnormalities, including VLCFA accumulation and plasmalogen reduction [72].
Association with neuropathological severity and altered peroxisomal distribution.
Temporal causality and reversibility. Contact-site disruption was not measured [72].
Select a reproducible biochemical phenotype and test whether correction improves neural function.
Human observational evidence; potentially contributory.
Parkinson's disease
Peroxisome-related lipid and quality-control mechanisms discussed in Refs. [16], [75].
A rationale to investigate peroxisomal participation in selected cellular states.
A primary peroxisomal lesion in typical PD is not established by these sources.
Measure peroxisomal function directly and distinguish it from mitochondrial-toxin injury.
Mechanistic literature; causal position uncertain.
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Peroxisomal involvement is discussed within a broader oxidative and metabolic disease context [16].
A hypothesis requiring direct testing.
General ROS and lipid abnormalities do not establish a peroxisomal mechanism.
Demonstrate a peroxisomal phenotype and selective rescue before attributing treatment benefit.
Direct disease-specific evidence remains limited.
Kleefstra syndrome
NMDAR-associated network dysfunction [27]; altered LDHA expression and toxicant sensitivity in cortical neurospheres [5].
Developmental and metabolic vulnerability in the studied models.
Basal ROS elevation, peroxisomal lipid flux, and peroxisome biogenesis were not established by these observations.
Use direct peroxisomal assays, independent donors and isogenic comparisons before testing a causal rescue hypothesis.
Hypothesis-generating for peroxisomal involvement.
Primary peroxisomal disorders
Genetic and biochemical defects in biogenesis, transport or individual enzymes [45], [65], [69], [83].
Causality for the affected peroxisomal pathway.
Biochemical defects and reversibility differ by disorder and developmental stage.
Match the construct to the missing function. Antioxidant activity alone does not restore all lipid pathways.
Genetic and biochemical causal evidence.

Artificial-peroxisome benchmark[85]
PMOXA–PDMS–PMOXA triblock-copolymer polymersomes incorporating OmpF channel proteins
Encapsulated Cu/Zn-superoxide dismutase (SOD) with lactoperoxidase (LPO); catalase (CAT)
Do not infer a targeting ligand from the term artificial peroxisome.
OmpF-mediated substrate transport; Substrate access with retention of macromolecular catalyst is the relevant design principle.
HeLa cells exposed to oxidative stress.
A patient-derived neural efficacy result is not established by the supplied summary.
Do not assign a neural efficacy value or specific ligand until the primary paper is checked.
Targeted nanoorganelle benchmark[19]
PDMS29-b-PMOXA10 diblocks, with PEG4–N3 end-functionalized chains for click coupling.
Encapsulated lactoperoxidase (LPO).
Arginine-rich cell-penetrating peptide (RR)4(KLL)2KGKC; not a CNS-selective receptor ligand.
Melittin pores. Optimized CPP-bearing vesicles had a reported hydrodynamic diameter of 140 ± 1 nm.
K562 myelogenous leukaemia cells challenged with H2O2.
No neural model tested. ESR indicated intracellular ROS attenuation in K562 cells.
Direct material/cargo/transport benchmark; cell penetration does not establish BBB transport or neural selectivity.
Non-vesicular artificial peroxisome[87]
Branched DNA with pH-responsive i-motif sequences and ceria nanoparticles.
Ceria with SOD-, catalase- and peroxidase-like activities; not encapsulated natural enzymes.
Intracellular assembly; no CNS-cell-selective ligand established here.
Acidic endolysosomal conditions trigger larger assemblies and support retention.
Living-cell oxidative-stress experiments.
The study establishes cellular ROS protection, not patient-derived AD/KS neural efficacy.
An experimental example of programmable assembly and selected redox catalysis, not full peroxisome replacement.
Non-CNS therapeutic example[88]
Mesenchymal stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles loaded with Mn3O4 nanozyme and further cloaked with platelet membrane (Mn@LPEV)
Mn3O4 nanozyme with immobilized lactate oxidase (LOX)
Platelet-membrane-based biomimetic targeting combined with a lactate-responsive delivery design for injured myocardium
MSC-EV encapsulation of Mn3O4 followed by platelet-membrane cloaking and LOX immobilization
Myocardial injury and heart-repair context.
Cardiac benefit cannot be treated as a neural or BBB efficacy result.
Relevant in vivo indication context, but detailed material claims must be checked against the primary paper.
Peroxisomal localization precedent[89]
Supramolecular structures formed from pyrene-labelled peptide amphiphiles.
Fluorescent nanoprobe; not a therapeutic multienzyme compartment.
C-terminal Ser–Lys–Leu (SKL) peroxisome-targeting sequence; sequence and assembly structure affect localization.
Self-assembly and localization.
Mammalian-cell localization; the accessible primary abstract does not specify the cell line.
Localization is not evidence of neuroprotection or metabolic rescue.
A targeting-method precedent, not an artificial-peroxisome efficacy benchmark.
Mitochondrial design precedent[90]
Designed multiblock peptide amphiphiles forming ellipsoidal nanoparticles.
Bioactive peptide architecture; no peroxisomal enzyme cargo.
Mitochondrial VDAC1–HK-II complex.
Self-assembly, cellular uptake and organelle-associated interaction targeting.
Melanoma inhibition.
Not a neural efficacy study and not direct peroxisome evidence.
Antitumour disruption of a protein interaction is not equivalent to restoring neuronal homeostasis.
Review-level context[86]
Multiple membrane-cloaked catalyst classes are reviewed.
Heterogeneous natural enzymes and enzyme-mimetic catalysts.
Several membrane sources and targeting approaches. (e.g., neutrophil- or erythrocyte-membrane-based delivery)
Review synthesis; no single platform or uniform transport measurement.
Multiple biomedical applications reviewed. (e.g., 3xTg-AD mice, MPTP-induced PD mice)
Neural studies discussed in the review must be traced to their individual primary papers.
This article is a review, not one experimental in vivo benchmark.

tables.label: Table 4
tables.caption: Functional comparison of peroxisome-related therapeutic platform concepts.
rows: Platform
Composition and cargo
ROS handling and lipid function
Targeting and uptake
Transport or localization
Potential advantage
Principal limitation
Developmental status
Natural biological peroxisome
Endogenous organelle with native membrane, transporters and metabolic enzymes [63], [65].
Both oxidant production and detoxification; pathway-specific lipid metabolism.
Endogenous organelle maintenance differs from uptake of an isolated organelle.
Native protein import and metabolite exchange; integrity may change after isolation.
Biological architecture and a broad endogenous enzyme repertoire.
Isolation purity, viability of cargo, functional stability, delivery and batch variability.
Native biology is established; CNS therapeutic transplantation is not established by the cited evidence.
Engineered biological peroxisome
Biological organelle modified genetically or chemically; cargo is design-dependent [84], [91].
Intended modification of selected native functions; retained activity must be measured.
In situ modification and exogenous delivery are different interventions.
Biological membrane and localization machinery, subject to engineering-related changes.
Can retain organelle architecture while modifying a defined function.
Perturbation tools are not replacements; complexity and delivery remain major barriers.
Experimental tools and platform concepts; no integrated patient-derived CNS efficacy benchmark here.
Membrane-bounded artificial peroxisome
Lipid, polymer or hybrid compartment with specified enzymes or catalysts [19], [85], [92], [93], [94].
Selected catalytic reactions. Antioxidant loading does not establish VLCFA or plasmalogen pathway restoration.
Endocytosis with optional ligands; specificity requires matched controls.
Permeability must permit substrate access and retain active cargo; intracellular destination is mechanism-dependent.
Control of composition, transport, active loading and surface chemistry.
Transport limitation, leakage, endolysosomal fate, immune effects and incomplete biomimicry.
Preclinical artificial-organelle evidence; integrated AD/KS iPSC neural validation remains unestablished in the examples reviewed.
Non-vesicular peroxisome-mimetic assembly
Catalytic material in a programmed scaffold, exemplified by DNA–ceria [87].
Enzyme-like redox catalysis; no complete native lipid network.
Uptake and intracellular assembly can control retention.
No native peroxisomal membrane or matrix-import machinery.
Programmable assembly and persistent selected catalytic activity.
Catalyst persistence, assembly heterogeneity and limited correspondence to a natural organelle.
Cellular proof of concept; CNS therapeutic efficacy requires separate evidence.
Conventional antioxidant nanocarrier
Lipidic, polymeric, inorganic or hybrid carrier containing a drug, enzyme or nanozyme [156], [157], [158].
Delivery or catalysis of selected antioxidants; activity may overlap with artificial-peroxisome constructs.
Established carrier-design approaches; CNS selectivity is formulation-specific.
Release, cellular uptake or local catalysis, depending on mechanism.
Potentially simpler formulation and a useful matched comparator.
Uncontrolled exposure, nonspecific effects or limited retention may still occur.
Maturity varies widely by product; nanocarrier precedent does not establish efficacy of a CNS peroxisome-inspired system.

tables.label: Table 5
tables.caption: Oxidative-stress paradigms and controls for neural biomaterial evaluation.
rows: Paradigm and purpose
Exposure or calibration
Disease context
Evidence status
Essential controls
Useful endpoints
Limit on interpretation
Baseline disease phenotype
No exogenous stress. Define differentiation stage, medium composition and sampling times before treatment.
Proposed first step in all disease-specific evaluations.
Matched control donors, isogenic comparison when available, vehicle and empty material.
Peroxisomal import and lipid function, redox state, survival and neural function.
A baseline disease difference must be reproducible before assigning disease-specific rescue.
Acute H2O2 challenge
Example pilot screen: 1–100 μM for 0.5–2 h, followed by washout and 24–48 h observation. Recalibrate for each model.
AD, PD, ALS (acute injury modeling)
Proposed calibration range, not a validated universal protocol or an estimate of brain H2O2 exposure.
Stress alone, extracellular free catalase, matched active cargo, empty material, catalytically inactive comparator if physically matched.
Peroxide handling, oxidative damage, recovery and viability; carrier/cargo integrity.
Can favour extracellular scavenging. Protection during co-exposure does not prove intracellular delivery.
Paraquat toxicant sensitivity
72 h exposure; differences at 10 and 30 μM; reported EC50 4.8 μM (KS) and 23.7 μM (control) [5].
KS coritcal neurosphere
Published model-specific anchor. These are sensitivity results, not recommended chronic treatment concentrations.
Matched neuronal maturity and spheroid size, control genotype, vehicle and cell-free assay controls.
Dose–response viability and oxidative injury with orthogonal functional measures.
Redox cycling is not peroxisome-specific. A single patient/control comparison does not establish population-level KS biology.
Rotenone challenge
72 h; differences at 0.01 and 0.1 μM; reported EC50 0.11 μM (KS) and 0.23 μM (control) [5].
KS neurosphere
Published compound- and maturation-dependent sensitivity example.
Solvent control, matched maturation, stress alone, antioxidant and mitochondrial mechanism controls.
Respiratory function, mitochondrial potential, oxidative damage and survival.
Complex I inhibition does not establish a primary peroxisomal defect.
Gradual antioxidant withdrawal
Published example: B27 minus antioxidants in DMEM/F12; longitudinal neurite imaging for 13 days, with 14-day screening [42].
AD, PD, ALS (aging-associated modeling)
Healthy-donor iPSC-derived neuron model, not a patient-derived ALS efficacy validation.
Matched antioxidant-containing medium, matched cell density and medium exchange, positive rescue comparator.
Longitudinal neurite response, lipid peroxidation, survival and mechanism-specific rescue.
Medium and cell density strongly affect injury; report and verify the actual plating density.
Disease-associated protein or inflammatory challenge
Use a model-specific dose–time matrix. Specify protein species and assembly state, or cytokine/LPS composition. No universal concentration is assigned.
All contexts (multifactorial modelling)
Proposed model-dependent validation; disease relevance must be demonstrated.
Preparation/vehicle controls, appropriate inactive or nonpathological comparator, composition-matched coculture and targeting controls.
Cell-specific injury, inflammatory response, neural activity and peroxisomal function.
A generic inflammatory or aggregation assay cannot establish a disease-specific peroxisomal mechanism.
Peroxisome-specific perturbation and rescue
Choose a defined biogenesis, transport or enzyme defect and a calibrated genetic/biochemical perturbation. Avoid a universal knockdown level.
KS (intrinsic vulnerability)
Proposed causal test, informed by genetically defined models [45].
Isogenic correction or rescue, non-targeting control, pathway-appropriate lipid or enzyme comparator.
Protein import, relevant lipid flux, compartment-specific redox response and neural function.
Marker expression alone is insufficient; rescue should link the biochemical defect to function.
tables.footnotes: Note: All exposures are in vitro. Published examples and proposed pilot ranges are labelled separately. Concentration, duration, medium, maturity, model geometry and recovery determine the biological exposure. For every material: report both material amount and active catalytic units, use empty and ligand-free controls where relevant, and test optical/chemical assay interference. A lower ROS-probe signal alone is not efficacy. For preloading experiments, wash away extracellular material before challenge when testing intracellular protection, and compare with simultaneous addition. Confirm retained intracellular activity.Abbreviations: AD, Alzheimer's disease; PD, Parkinson's disease; ALS, Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; KS, Kleefstra syndrome; iPSC, induced pluripotent stem cell; LPS, lipopolysaccharide.

figures.caption: Proposed evaluation framework for peroxisome-inspired CNS biomaterials. (A) Disease selection distinguishes primary peroxisomal disorders, late-onset neurodegeneration, and KS as a hypothesis-generating developmental context. (B) Patient-derived neural systems enable disease phenotyping and measurement of peroxisomal function. Neural progenitor-derived spheroids and cerebral organoids are distinct model types. (C) Material composition, retained catalytic cargo, permeability, and validated surface ligands are selected for a defined mechanism. Antioxidant activity and lipid-metabolic replacement require different evidence. (D) Neural efficacy, BBB transport, animal pharmacology, safety, and manufacturing are evaluated through decision points with iteration between stages. Progression is conditional on reproducible target engagement, functional benefit, exposure, and acceptable safety. The diagram describes a proposed development process, not a validated therapeutic pipeline. Figure was created with BioRender.com.

figures.label: Fig. 2
figures.caption: Peroxisomal mechanisms and disease-specific interpretation. (A) Peroxisomes contribute to fatty acid processing, the initial steps of ether-lipid synthesis, and H2O2 production and removal. Their interactions with mitochondria involve metabolic and redox coupling, while plasmalogen biosynthesis also requires the endoplasmic reticulum. Shared fission machinery and reported contacts do not establish universal directional substrate or Ca2+ transfer. (B) Peroxisomal defects are causal in primary peroxisomal disorders; AD evidence is largely associative, the causal position in PD and ALS remains uncertain, and KS requires direct peroxisomal phenotyping. (C) A disease-associated defect must be linked to a specific material function and an independent functional outcome. Demonstrated antioxidant catalysis should be distinguished from proposed lipid-metabolic restoration. Arrows indicate relationships or proposed evaluation steps, not established causal chains in all diseases. Figure was created with BioRender.com.

figures.label: Fig. 3
figures.caption: Material design and catalytic transport in artificial peroxisomes. (A) Liposomal, polymeric, and hybrid membranes provide different options for composition, permeability, stability, and degradation. These properties require measurement for each formulation. (B) H2O2 must access catalase while active enzyme is retained. OmpF illustrates a pore-forming design precedent, not a validated component of every platform. SOD converts accessible superoxide to H2O2, requiring sufficient downstream peroxide removal. H2O2, superoxide, and hydroxyl radical are distinct chemical species with different transport and reaction behaviour. (C) Stimuli-responsive materials require an experimentally demonstrated link between trigger, structural response, and catalytic performance. (D) Relevant measurements include hydrodynamic size, charge, membrane mechanics, ligand density, active loading, leakage, permeability, and degradation. No universal size or charge optimum for CNS delivery is implied. Figure was created with BioRender.com.

figures.label: Fig. 4
figures.caption: Delivery barriers and mechanism-dependent intracellular fate. (A) Endothelial binding and uptake must be distinguished from productive BBB transcytosis and delivery of intact active material to brain parenchyma. Size, charge, ligand density, and deformability are variables to optimize, not fixed success criteria. Red schematic particles represent enzyme-containing constructs, not nucleic-acid cargo. (B) 3D organoid exposure may produce surface accumulation and radial concentration gradients. Bath exposure, perfusion, and microinjection test different delivery constraints. (C) Endocytosed material may remain active within endosomal compartments, escape to the cytosol, or undergo lysosomal loss. The required destination depends on substrate access and mechanism; proximity to a peroxisome does not demonstrate fusion or matrix import. (D) Neural, barrier, immune, and in vivo models address complementary questions. Uptake, functional efficacy, penetration, immune responses, pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and safety should be measured in the models appropriate to each endpoint.
